{{short description|Wreath product of cyclic group m and symmetrical group n}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''generalized symmetric group''' is the [[wreath product]] <math>S(m,n) := C_m \wr S_n</math> of the [[cyclic group]] of [[order (group theory)|order]] ''m'' and the [[symmetric group]] of order ''n''.

== Examples ==
* For <math>m=1,</math> the generalized symmetric group is exactly the ordinary symmetric group: <math>S(1,n) = S_n.</math>
* For <math>m=2,</math> one can consider the cyclic group of order 2 as positives and negatives (<math>C_2 \cong \{\pm 1\}</math>) and identify the generalized symmetric group <math>S(2,n)</math> with the [[signed symmetric group]].

== Representation theory ==
There is a natural [[group representation|representation]] of elements of <math>S(m,n)</math> as [[generalized permutation matrices]], where the nonzero entries are ''m''-th [[roots of unity]]: <math>C_m \cong \mu_m.</math>

The representation theory has been studied since {{Harv|Osima|1954}}; see references in {{Harv|Can|1996}}. As with the symmetric group, the representations can be constructed in terms of [[Specht module]]s; see {{Harv|Can|1996}}.

== Homology ==
The first [[group homology]] group – concretely, the [[abelianization]] – is <math>C_m \times C_2</math> (for ''m'' [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] this is [[isomorphic]] to <math>C_{2m}</math>): the <math>C_m</math> factors (which are all [[conjugacy class|conjugate]], hence must map identically in an [[abelian group]], since conjugation is trivial in an abelian group) can be mapped to <math>C_m</math> (concretely, by taking the product of all the <math>C_m</math> values), while the sign map on the symmetric group yields the <math>C_2.</math> These are independent, and generate the group, hence are the abelianization.

The second homology group – in classical terms, the [[Schur multiplier]] – is given by {{Harv|Davies|Morris|1974}}:
:<math>H_2(S(2k+1,n)) = \begin{cases} 1 & n < 4\\
\mathbf{Z}/2 & n \geq 4.\end{cases}</math>
:<math>H_2(S(2k+2,n)) = \begin{cases} 1 & n = 0, 1\\
\mathbf{Z}/2 & n = 2\\
(\mathbf{Z}/2)^2 & n = 3\\
(\mathbf{Z}/2)^3 & n \geq 4.
\end{cases}</math>
Note that it depends on ''n'' and the [[parity (mathematics)|parity]] of ''m:'' <math>H_2(S(2k+1,n)) \approx H_2(S(1,n))</math> and <math>H_2(S(2k+2,n)) \approx H_2(S(2,n)),</math> which are the Schur multipliers of the symmetric group and signed symmetric group.
